analysis.title: Stress-Testing The Perkini Report (Macro Picture, The Sequel)
key_insights: Follow-up to TS Lombard's AI crash scenario: baseline is $20 trillion of US equity wealth wiped out but only a mild US recession, comparable in size and duration to 1990 and 2001 and nothing like 2008-09. Credit losses in the AI ecosystem are estimated at $150-200bn.

The firm keeps its view on the direct effects of a crash. Multipliers on AI capex are small because most datacenter equipment is imported from Korea and Taiwan, so falling imports offset lower capex. Datacenter construction employs about 500k workers, rising to 800k if the boom runs 12 more months, and losing those jobs adds roughly 50bps to unemployment.

Four indirect risks could make the baseline too benign: macro reflexivity, larger wealth effects, AI automation accelerating during the downturn (slower, jobless recovery), and inflation limiting the Fed's response, especially if the crash follows a supply shock.
The estimated hit to employment comes close to triggering the Sahm Rule, under which a rise in unemployment of more than 0.5 percentage points usually keeps rising.

Wealth effects are assumed weak because the link between household net worth and the saving rate has broken since the GFC. The wealth coefficient in a consumption regression is no longer statistically significant in recent samples, and the marginal propensity to consume from equities is less than half that of housing wealth.

Reasons the wealth effect could be larger: the assumed 40% fall in US tech stocks and 20% fall in the rest could be exceeded or spread to real estate, confidence effects from a selloff, balance-sheet and cost-of-capital channels (collateral, WACC), and US market cap to GDP now almost double its Dotcom level.

On the Fed, the firm expects the AI shock to shift the Fed's focus to employment and expects rate cuts to work because real estate and consumer durables are held back by current rates. Bond yields would rise only if the selloff came from a 1970s-style supply shock, such as escalation in the Iran conflict.

Global decoupling is expected in two phases: an initial synchronized risk-off with all stocks falling, then investor discrimination in which euro area and UK equities outperform, especially in USD terms. Bonds in all major markets would perform well and the dollar would weaken.

Timing: the crash start is still assumed for early 2028, as a scenario and not a forecast. The firm does not see the crash as imminent because hyperscalers are not cutting capex, GPU rental prices are resilient, AI ecosystem earnings have not disappointed, and the Fed has raised rates by 25bps. Baseline assumes 125bps of tightening over the next year.

The firm gives reasons why three things that could extend the boom are unlikely to help. An energy price plunge would lift real incomes and keep the Fed hiking. There is no evidence yet of AI productivity gains. A labour market setback is unlikely because US employment recoveries tend to continue until a new shock arrives.

The firm leans toward the commoditization view of AI. Estimated token price elasticity is -0.6 to -0.9, below the Jevons paradox threshold needed for 'everyone makes money', and high fixed costs, low marginal costs and intense competition from Chinese open-weight models (about six months behind the frontier) tend to produce oversupply.

About $500bn of GPUs are still waiting to come online. The firm expects current bottlenecks to turn into a glut, as at the Dotcom peak. If chip prices fall, Nvidia could not backstop the ecosystem, and the firm says that hope has already suffered a setback in recent weeks.

A soft landing for hyperscaler capex requires capex to fall more slowly than new non-tech revenue enters the ecosystem. The firm sees this as implausible, because it would need a very large rise in AI subscription revenue and would make the AI boom a historical outlier. Hockey-stick charts such as US tech capex to GDP and Taiwanese and Korean semiconductor exports rarely soft land.
Conclusion: the original analysis holds, and if forced to choose the firm leans toward the bears, because the bull case amounts to 'this time is different'.

sector_views.rationale: Expects an AI investment crash around 2028, with a 40% decline in US tech stocks assumed in the scenario, and leans toward commoditization of datacenter owners and model developers.
After an initial synchronized selloff, expects these markets to outperform in a decoupling phase because they did not participate in the AI boom and have lower tech share than at Dotcom.

tension_points.theme: AI crash timing and soft landing
tension_points.bull_case: Earnings are still growing rapidly, GPU rental prices are resilient, and hyperscalers are honouring capex commitments. Bulls point to a Jevons paradox in which falling token prices lift total spending, with Nvidia as backstop (Gavin Baker scenario).
tension_points.bear_case: Token elasticity of -0.6 to -0.9 is below the Jevons threshold, GPU supply of $500bn is waiting, and AI has high fixed costs and intense competition that point to commoditization and bankruptcies.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Hyperscalers cutting planned datacenter investment, or AI ecosystem earnings disappointing, would signal the crash is under way. A rise in token elasticity above the Jevons threshold would support the bull case.

tension_points.theme: Wealth effects of an AI crash
tension_points.bull_case: The wealth coefficient in consumption regressions is no longer statistically significant after the GFC, and the marginal propensity to consume from equities is less than half that of housing.
tension_points.bear_case: Equity declines could exceed the assumed 40% and 20%, spread to real estate, and market cap to GDP is almost double its Dotcom level, which magnifies the hit to wealth.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A crash that spreads to real estate, or a market decline larger than the assumed 40% in tech and 20% elsewhere, would make the weak wealth effect assumption too benign.

tension_points.theme: Fed response to an AI crash
tension_points.bull_case: The Fed would pivot to the employment side of its mandate and cut rates, and cuts would crowd in real estate and consumer durables.
tension_points.bear_case: Inflation risk could prevent cuts, and the bond market could react badly, particularly if the crash follows a 1970s-style supply shock.
tension_points.what_invalidates: An AI selloff triggered by a supply shock such as a further escalation in the Iran conflict would limit Fed easing.

theme_stances.key_argument: The firm expects the AI boom to continue until about 2028 and then end, either naturally or through Fed hikes.
theme_stances.evidence: Either the boom ends of natural causes soon or the Fed eventually murders it with hikes.

theme_stances.key_argument: Token elasticity is below the Jevons threshold and AI economics point to oversupply and bankruptcies.
theme_stances.evidence: we lean towards the commoditization side of the AI debate

theme_stances.key_argument: After an initial synchronized selloff, euro area and UK equities outperform because they did not take part in the boom.
theme_stances.evidence: investor discrimination, where the decoupling thesis starts to gain traction
